description: Team J2000: high school students who compete in math olympiads and do research in particle physics and mathematics. For Space Apps 2026 we built Epoch, a time machine for NASA's SPHEREx sky.
summary: Using nothing more than a web browser, volunteers of Backyard Worlds have found nearby brown dwarfs, cold objects too small to shine as stars, by blinking between infrared sky images taken years apart. NASA's SPHEREx telescope photographs the entire sky in 102 infrared colors, but because each picture records a different color, blinking between them makes every ordinary star appear to change. We built Epoch, a web tool that puts that method back in anyone's hands: type a position, and it plays every SPHEREx picture of that spot in time order, read directly from the 1.18 million pictures in NASA's first SPHEREx data release. Comparing each picture only with pictures from the same detector removes a median 93% of the false changes, and a neural network in the browser marks the changes most likely to be real. On 147 real asteroid sightings, it found 71, more than any other method we tested. On the five challenge targets, Epoch detects WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, at 12.1σ, measures the distance to Epsilon Indi B from SPHEREx alone, and catches the pulsating giant R Draconis within 2.5 days of its predicted peak. Across the sky, it has already measured methane in 16 cold brown dwarfs for which no spectrum has been published.
details:
Epoch is a time machine for the SPHEREx sky. A visitor types any position, and the site reads every SPHEREx picture of that spot straight from NASA's public archive and plays them in date order. Nothing has to be installed and there is no server: an index of all 1,179,406 pictures in the first data release lets the browser download only the small patch it needs from each file.

SPHEREx photographs each star at a different infrared wavelength every time, so a plain blink, the method volunteers have used to find nearby brown dwarfs in older surveys, shows stars changing when nothing has. Epoch compares each picture only with pictures from the same detector, which removed a median 93% of these false changes across 20 random fields. A small neural network running in the browser then marks likely real changes, and keeps a mark only where SPHEREx's two simultaneous pictures agree, so cosmic rays and bad pixels drop out. On new fields crossed by real asteroids it found 71 of 147 sightings, more than any other method we tested. Clicking any source shows its spectrum and tests it for the methane absorption of a cold brown dwarf; on 78 brown dwarfs of known type, every methane call it made was correct.

With these tools we detected WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, at 12.1σ, and measured the distance to Epsilon Indi B from SPHEREx positions alone. Across the sky we found 16 cold brown dwarfs and 7 candidate emission-line stars with no published classification, all downloadable for follow-up, which we plan to investigate further!

Epoch is meant to put SPHEREx in the hands of the volunteers who search survey images, of students and teachers, and of astronomers who want to check a position before downloading data. It works on a phone, in English and Spanish, and a new data release needs one index build and a one-line change.

Its creative step is to treat the changing color of each picture as the problem to solve, and to use SPHEREx's own design, simultaneous pictures on two detectors, to separate real changes from artifacts. The site is plain JavaScript on GitHub Pages. The analysis runs in Python (NumPy, pandas, Astropy), and the network was trained in JAX on a laptop. Reference data come from Gaia DR3, WISE and JPL Horizons.

The factor we weighed most was trust because we made sure every method was tested on real objects and that every false-alarm rate was measured against ordinary stars or empty sky.
